title: Latches and flip-flops
subtitle: Combinational logic has no memory. Feed an output back to an input and you get a circuit that remembers.

seq.title: Memory from feedback
seq.body: A combinational output depends only on the present inputs. A sequential circuit’s output also depends on its state — what happened before — stored in latches or flip-flops. The simplest memory is two cross-coupled NOR (or NAND) gates: each output feeds the other’s input, so the pair holds whichever state it was last pushed into.

sr.title: The SR latch
sr.body: Inputs S (set) and R (reset): S = 1 forces Q = 1; R = 1 forces Q = 0; S = R = 0 holds the previous Q; S = R = 1 is forbidden (both outputs collapse, and releasing both at once is unpredictable). Toggle S and R below and watch Q remember.
sr.steps: Start with Q = 0. Set S = 1, R = 0 → Q = 1. Return S to 0. With S = R = 0 the latch holds Q = 1: memory.

d.title: Gated latch and the D flip-flop
d.body: A D latch is transparent while the enable is high — its output follows D. A D flip-flop is edge-triggered: it samples D only at the clock’s rising edge and holds it until the next. Edge triggering makes whole systems predictable: every flip-flop changes at the same instant.

jkt.title: JK and T flip-flops
jkt.body:
J KNext Q
0 0Q (hold)
0 10 (reset)
1 01 (set)
1 1Q′ (toggle)

The JK fixes the forbidden state by making 1,1 toggle. Tie J and K together and you get a T flip-flop: T = 1 toggles every clock, which halves the frequency.
jkt.steps: A T flip-flop with T = 1 is clocked at 8 MHz. Q toggles once per clock, so one full Q cycle takes two clocks.

time.title: Setup and hold time
time.body: D must be stable for a setup time before the clock edge and a hold time after it, or the flip-flop may go metastable (neither 0 nor 1 for a while). The clock period must cover clock-to-Q delay + logic delay + setup time.
time.steps: t_cq = 2 ns, logic = 8 ns, setup = 1 ns. Minimum period = 11 ns, so f_max ≈ 91 MHz.

tbl.title: Characteristic tables and excitation
tbl.body: The characteristic equation gives the next state: D: Q⁺ = D; T: Q⁺ = T⊕Q; JK: Q⁺ = JQ′ + K′Q. The excitation table runs the other way: given the wanted transition Q → Q⁺, what inputs are needed? For JK, 0→1 needs J = 1 (K = X); 1→0 needs K = 1 (J = X). Used when designing counters and state machines.
